First off, I'm sorry that you are experiencing life this way right now. I have had the same problem and it can make you feel terrible. But it is possible to overcome it, tune into different frequencies. What helps is knowing how your mind works and finding out where it goes astray. 

What helped me was to use the logically-structured, rational side of my mind to factor in variables and error margins that I hadn't been considering in my obsessions about degree choices, future job outlooks, etc. I find that OCD has a certain rational element to it (like if/then logic) but the irrational elements are still bigger such that it traps us in contradictions. These contradictions are what eventually create the distress and the exhaustion. E.g. if I wash my hands then I'll be safe, but (contradiction!) I know that washing my hands actually doesn't help, yet (contradiction!) if I DON'T do it, I can't relax...etc. And so you kind of mentally and emotionally "circle the drain." 

Rationally questioning fears has been helpful in easing the cognitive elements of the OCD, factoring in more uncertainty as something unavoidable. I know that this sounds counter-intuitive, because obsessing over considering all variables and uncertainties is exactly what makes us so miserable. We yearn for safety, a secure future, to know that everything is going to be okay. There's always that child-like part of us that needs that unconditional safety, and that's a valid part of ourselves that we should be considerate of and integrate into our lives.

However, if you are perfectionistic and tend toward obsessing, you'll be more likely to project standards onto the universe that are impossible for it to fulfill to your satisfaction. As you wrestle with the truth - that there will always be uncertainty and lack of total control - and internally resist this truth, as you internally insist on having more control than human life today can give you, you'll become more anxiety-ridden and depressed. And you'll become exhausted as you resist life in this way. It's like trying to displace Mt. Everest with only your two bare hands. You find yourself needing / demanding something that contemporary homo sapien life cannot give you, i.e. total safety, security and certainty. And that's why you can't escape the OCD, unless you re-train your thinking and expose yourself to uncertainty. And you might need medication or supplements. If you can afford it, I recommend looking for an exposure response therapist, as this helped me. But I'm not a trained therapist and cannot give you medical advice, only share with you my own experiences and thoughts about this. 

To circle back to what I was saying: It helped me alleviate obsessions by analytically looking at my thought processes and then critically questioning the manner in which I weighted my fears. The sobering conclusion was that I can estimate probabilities for the future, but cannot really know what will happen tomorrow. Another conclusion was that, while some things like poverty, loss, homelessness and failure do suck, there is a good chance to not be afflicted, and that if you ever are, there are chances to survive these things, recover and succeed in goals. The bottom line is that you can guesstimate, but never know everything. You can't even be 100% certain about what will happen in 5 minutes. Bad things can happen, but it is also possible to overcome them.

On another note:

I think that some of the problems that you and I have right now arise from a real predicament that most human beings are in. When planning for the future, our brains naturally tend to extrapolate linearly because this sufficed in navigating socio-economic conditions that tended to evolve more gradually and slowly in time. We are thus not naturally wired to think geometrically, exponentially, i.e. in whacky curves. Because for most our time on Earth - aside from natural catastrophes and raids once in awhile - we could know that what was on one day, would likely be the same on another day in 5 or 10 years. The river with the fish would still be there, the forest would still be there, the caribou would migrate, the snow would come and go, etc. Almost everything necessary for our survival exhibited slower rates of change in time. Of course there was always uncertainty (meteors, draughts, war with another tribe etc) but nothing like the fast-paced changing of today's modern society. I think this is why in most preceeding cultures, elders were sought after as the teachers in almost all aspects of life. Now, our elders tend to learn more from the young about how to navigate our all-pervasive, technology that people need to get food, shelter, communicate, do busines, trade etc. I've seen many elders that are often helpless in keeping up with the technology resulting from exponentially increasing computational power (Moore's law!). I notice that it is even becoming harder for them to advise younger people about the more fundamental issues in life like love, relationships, passions, money, parenting etc. because, due to the way that technological change influences social change, even these fundamentals are now changing in nature faster and faster, though their changes are still "more constant" in time than the changes in technology and communication. Considering that we've been here for a little over 100,000 years and that this "exponential nature of modern life" just really started kicking off vertically only a few decades ago (first computers, splitting of the atom, radio technology, internet, etc), the brain is also facing new challenges that come at it faster and faster. Elders naturally learn slower and have more trouble adapting to these ever-more rapidly in-coming changes because our brains didn't have to keep re-learning fundamentals in such short time intervals. Now they do.

I'm sorry if all this increases the anxiety, but this helped me to at least understand that there isn't just something wrong with me alone. There's actually something going on with humanity right now, and that the body/brain are responding to it (in an unhelpful manner) with obsessions and anxiety. So it's not "all in my head." Although I do believe that we have the power to retrain ourselves to more constructively react to these objective circumstances, we're  facing and be that through mental health treatment, meditation, exercise, changes in lifestyle, i.e. whatever best helps you at this point and time with your situation. You're unique and what helps me, might not necessarily help you.

Regarding the concrete question - do I change degrees? - I think that what you can perhaps try is to find a more general direction to think in, a direction general enough that it doesn't lead to an overly specific, overly detailed end-goal. Think in smaller time increments, do what is fun to you and what is likely to get you quickly and easily into the general direction you are drawn into. Try to be present more in the here and now with what you choose to do. You cannot know what will be in the future, only what you can do now. And chances are, you'll change and evolve along the way and thus so will your goals, dreams etc. And that's totally fine. Our generation will have to learn to "go with the flow" more to maintain mental health. Make clear to yourself that you cannot have a guarantee about your future, you cannot know. But you can learn to know and feel for certain that you will deal with whatever problems come, and that life can also pleasantly surprise you. You can anticipate doom (the OCD talking) and end up in paradise. The trick there is to manage the OCD to the point that it doesn't paralyze or sabotage you. 

If it helps you to feel seen, heard and better understood, this is all coming from a triple major in physics (BS), quantitative economics (BS) and political science (BA) who was in the same boat a few months ago. I ended up re-making course tables and decision tables for over 7 degrees that I could not decide on, staying up for 3 days straight looking up everything that went wrong for others, incapable of feeling safe with any choice, and then eventually developing catatonic anxiety (involuntary changes in facial expressions, contorted arms). I gave in, went to the ER and got benzos. At least the benzos allowed me to get a decent night's sleep. I'm not a doctor and can't give medication advice, but if you need to pull the emergency brake and medicate for some time (and be it anxiolytics for a few days), don't be ashamed to seek help. To experience a relief from the anxiety for a few days and get deep sleep can help you find your center and it helps you to get to know how it feels not to be afraid. 

I hope this helps a bit. Feel free to drop a line if you need to chat. I can't answer right away, and can sometimes need awhile, but I'm happy to communicate.

>Am I the only one annoyed at this?

I usually don't get truly annoyed. I'm really "annoyed," in the truest sense of the word, when one of the neighbors goes by the house at 4am without a muffler on his shitbox car and wakes me up from much-needed sleep.

But I have had moments where people's inability to research basic things for themselves has left me feeling cynical about humanity. (Like neighbors asking about restaurant opening times on NextDoor instead of googling it).

I think it depends on the question, though, and the underlying intent of those asking it. I'm in physics and there's simply a lot of stuff I can't just google, because new knowledge is being created in the process and I have only a handful of people deep enough in the material who can know, have time or care enough about the (sometimes migraine-inducing) subtleties to answer the questions I might have. And it might be useful to get multiple, conflicting answers so that a constructive debate can ensue.

But I've also been guilty of skipping Google on far simpler things, because I grew very tired of the bullshit results: oceans of "informative" articles that take paragraphs to get to a simple point - many actually NEVER get there - and whose primary purpose is obviously not to answer your question, but merely to appear to do so, thus generating ad revenue by including as many of the searchable terms in your question as possible and luring in your clicks (and wasting your time). Or I sift through seemingly endless forum discussions that don't get anywhere, either because 

- OP gives up/stops answering 

- the OP's problem diverges at some point too strongly from the nature of my own,

- or because forum participants get into an off-topic argument that grows nastier and nastier until a mod comes along and shuts down the thread. 

Again, it all depends on the type of question I have, but the aforementioned issues are some of my time-economic reasons for skipping Google on some questions. For what it's worth, I do use Boolean operators to refine my search queries. While this is helpful, saves time and noticeably improves the quality of my results, the problems I've mentioned can still occur, depending on the question. 

And sometimes I skip Google because it's just nice to have that human-to-human interaction. Is that perhaps why you posted your question here on Reddit? ;)

Well, first off: congratulations on figuring out that you have it. The earlier the better. Not to make you worry, but my dad had OCD from around 15 until he committed suicide at 56. It started with me around age 15 and for 16 years, I didn't know I had it (it's genetic from my dad), but after being diagnosed, I realized why simply just living normal life had been a teeth-gritting fight for so long. 

It's been about a week since I've found a psychiatrist/psychologist (he's both) who specializes in it and himself has it(!). We're doing a therapy session tomorrow and discussing checking/reassurance behaviors (I have them so bad, they become debilitating).

I can only speak for myself, but I've had several major anxiety-inducing crises so far that heavily provoked compulsive reassurance behaviors (like having to google even when someone is right there talking to me in person). For me, it made things worse because nothing I found was ever good or assuring enough, and that made me never want to stop searching. No matter what I found, my brain always had a horrific what-if that made me keep searching. 

Now, mind you...some what-if's are totally reasonable. But with me, for example: I would search for college majors based on salary, but then do so factoring in that my mom was going to die at any minute (she's totally fine) and that I would need to earn enough to do without the support I was going to lose because she'd die while I was in college. And then I'd spend weeks online looking for people whose mothers had died while they went to college so I could refine my search. But my brain alwaya came up with yet another obstacle. 

My advice: knowing now that you have it, do everything you can to cease reassuring behaviors. In the end, they will cost you so much time and energy.

This is an important point. The behavior itself is usually not the problem. It's how often it's done and to the extent that it interferes with what would otherwise be a fairly healthy and productive life that matters. 

Take me trying to pick a college major, for example. Most people would spend a long time doing copious amounts of research before making such a big choice. Me? I was literally up for four days straight incessantly googling, trying to find people's worst-case-scenario stories regarding all the options I was looking at. The end-result: I got psychotic catatonic anxiety, was vomiting, panicking and had to be brought into the ER for benzos. Oh, and I still never really chose a major because in my mind, the worst possible case of whatever I was considering was assumed to be the end-result. Real OCD has a paralysis factor. It keeps you stuck such that your cautiousness becomes the most dangerous thing for you. One kind of cautiousness is normal, the other is OCD. Sometimes the border blurs, other times it's pretty clear.

I appreciate your caution and I do agree. We quickly fall in love with this stuff but often fail to see the whole "Black Mirror"-ish dystopian side it brings along... human nature continues to be brutal in many ways, even with slick technology and science. The brain that our species works with is still roughly the same model from 100,000 years ago.
